Ef fi cacy of High-Flow Nasal Cannula vs Standard Oxygen Therapy or Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure in Children with Respiratory Distress: A Meta-Analysis
Jian Luo, MD, PhD 1 , Trevor Duke, MD, FRACP 2 , Mohammod Jobayer Chisti, MBBS, MMed, PhD 2,3 , Elizabeth Kepreotes, PhD 4 , Valerie Kalinowski, MD, MHA 5 , and Jie Li, MS, RRT-NPS, RRT-ACCS 6

Objectives To evaluate the efficacy of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy in providing respiratory support of children with acute lower respiratory infection (ALRI), hypoxemia, and respiratory distress.

Study design Weperformed a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials that compared HFNC and standard flow oxygen therapy or nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) and reported treatment failure as an outcome. Data were synthesized using Mann-Whitney U test.

Results Compared with standard oxygen therapy, HFNC significantly reduced treatment failure (risk ratio [RR] 0.49, 95% CI 0.40-0.60, P < .001) in children with mild hypoxemia (arterial pulse oximetry [SpO2] >90% on room air). HFNC had an increased risk of treatment failure compared with nCPAP in infants age 1-6 months with severe hypoxemia (SpO2 <90% on room air or SpO2 >90% on supplemental oxygen) (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.17-2.67, P =.007). Nosignificant differences were found in intubation rates and mortality between HFNC and standard oxygen therapy or nCPAP. HFNC had a lower risk of nasal trauma compared with nCPAP (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.77, P = .009). Conclusions Among children <5 years of age with ALRI, respiratory distress, and mild hypoxemia, HFNC reduced the risk of treatment failure when compared with standard oxygen therapy. However, nCPAP was associated with a lower risk of treatment failure than HFNC in infants age 1-6 months with ALRI, moderate-to-severe respiratory distress, and severe hypoxemia. No differences were found in intubation and mortality between HFNC and standard oxygen therapy or nCPAP. (J Pediatr 2019; -:1-10) .

A cute bronchiolitis and pneumonia are the major causes of respiratory failure in pediatrics, of whom 15% may require respiratory support and intensive care unit (ICU) care because of worsening respiratory distress. 1,2 The global mortality annually is estimated as 1.3 million for pneumonia in children younger than 5 years, including 200 000 for bronchiolitis. 1,3

Oxygen supplementation is recommended by the World Health Organization if the arterial pulse oximetry (SpO2) is <90% in children with acute lower respiratory infection (ALRI), based on the evidence that oxygenation improvement is associated with reduced mortality. 4,5 This is also consistent with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommendation. 6

Standard flow oxygen therapy delivers oxygen through a standard nasal cannula at a rate of 0.5-1 L/min for infants, 1-2 L/min for children younger than 2 years of age, and up to a maximum of 4 L/min for children over 2 years of age. 7,8 Standard flow rates do not require humidification. Higher flow rates require humidification because of the drying effect of unhumidified cold oxygen on nasal secretions and the respiratory mucosa. 9-11

Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) combines supplemental oxygen and a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), typically of 4-10 cm H2O. nCPAP has been shown to reduce the duration of ventilation and hospital stay in infants with severe bronchiolitis. 12 However, the availability From the 1 Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, West China School of Medicine and West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China; 2 Center for International Child Health, The University of Melbourne Department of Pediatrics, Murdoch Children's Research Institute and Intensive Care Unit, Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; 3 Intensive Care Unit, Dhaka Hospital, Nutrition and Clinical Services Division, International Center for Diarrheal Disease Research, Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; 4 John Hunter Children's Hospital, Hunter Medical Research Institute, University of Newcastle GrowUpWell Priority Research Center, Australia; 5 Pediatric ICU, Rush University Children's Hospital, and 6 Division of Respiratory Care, Department of Cardiopulmonary Sciences, Rush University Medical Center, Rush University, Chicago, IL

of nCPAP is limited in low-resource settings because of the requirement for clinical and technical skills, equipment, and maintenance. 13

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy is currently a popular modality of respiratory support in pediatric care. HFNC delivers warmed and humidified oxygen (usually with a blended mix with air) at a higher flow than the patient's inspiratory flow, typically 1-2 L/kg/min. 14 Observational studies suggest HFNC may improve oxygenation and reduce the need for mechanical ventilation in neonates and children with respiratory distress. 15-18 A recent meta-analysis and systematic review of HFNC in bronchiolitis revealed that HFNC reduced treatment failure compared with standard oxygen therapy, but increased treatment failure compared with nCPAP. 19 However, this meta-analysis only included studies of bronchiolitis, and the evidence for children with pneumonia and other ALRI who have hypoxemia and respiratory distress is less clear. Moreover, 3 randomized controlled trials 20-22 have been published between June 2018 and March 2019, which was beyond the search period and not included in the previous meta-analysis. 19

Younger age has been identified as an independent risk for HFNC treatment failure in some studies, 13,23 but not in others. 10 Thus, a subgroup analysis of the effect of age on the HFNC treatment outcomes is important.

Based on this uncertainty, we performed this meta-analysis to further evaluate the clinical benefits of HFNC in children up to the age of 5 years with ALRI, hypoxemia, and respiratory distress. (PROSPERO registration number: CRD42018103516).
Methods

A search of the published literature was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Medline, CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, American College of Physician, for studies conducted until March of 2019, using the following keywords: ('highflow nasal cannul*' OR 'high flow cannul*' OR 'high flow oxygen therapy' OR 'high flow oxygen' OR 'high flow therapy' OR 'HFNC' OR 'high flow high humidity nasal cannul*' OR 'high-flow warm humidified oxygen' OR 'hot humidified high-flow' OR 'continuous positive airway pressure' OR 'CPAP' OR 'nasal continuous positive airway pressure' OR 'nCPAP' OR 'oxygen therapy' OR 'oxygen supplementation' OR 'oxygen delivery' OR 'conventional oxygen therapy' OR 'COT') AND ('infan*' OR 'neonat*' OR 'child*'). Publication type was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) regardless of the language. We also reviewed the reference list in each identified study and manually searched the relevant trials to identify all other eligible studies.
Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) RCTs comparing HFNC and nCPAP or standard oxygen therapy in children aged from 29 days to 5 years, with

ALRI and respiratory distress and the need for supplemental oxygen; (2) studies reported at least one of the following outcomes: treatment failure rate, intubation rate, and mortality; and (3) other reporting outcomes included adverse events, duration of hypoxemia, and need for oxygen, and length of hospital or ICU stay.
We did not include studies that were retrospective, crossover, observational, cohort, or case-control. Study protocols, review articles, abstracts, editorials, and animal studies were also excluded.
Study Selection and Data Extraction

Two independent investigators were assigned to extract the data from the eligible studies by screening titles and abstracts and reviewing full texts. Data from the included studies were recorded in a standard form recommended by Cochrane. 24 We contacted the corresponding or first author to request the subgroup data specifically for infants age 29 days to 6 months, 6-12 months, and children age 1-5 years or if there were any missing data. Any disagreement was resolved by mutual consensus in the presence of all investigators.
Quality Assessment

For the assessment of risk of bias in estimating the study outcomes, we used the Cochrane risk of bias tool. 24 Each study was assessed for (1) random sequence generation (selection bias); (2) allocation concealment (selection bias); (3) blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias); (4) blinding of related outcomes assessment (detection bias); (5) incomplete outcome data (attrition bias); (6) selective reporting (reporting bias); and (7) other biases. Two investigators conducted the quality assessment for the study methodology, independently and in duplicate. Any divergence was resolved by mutual consensus in the presence of a third investigator.
Statistical Analyses

Continuous variables were shown as mean and SD, and dichotomous variables were reported as frequency and proportion. Forest plots were depicted using fixed-effects model algorithm in the absence of statistical heterogeneity; otherwise a random-effects model was adopted. We calculated mean difference (MD) and 95% CI for continuous data, and risk ratio (RR) and 95% CIs were calculated for dichotomous data; c 2 test and visual inspection of forest plots were used for the assessment of statistical heterogeneity, and P <.1 and I 2 >50% indicated significant heterogeneity. We also did subgroup analyses of infants age 1-6 months, 6-12 months, and children age 1-5 years between HFNC vs nCPAP or standard oxygen respectively in the primary outcomes.

Two independent investigators performed the statistical analysis using Cochrane systematic review software Review Manager (RevMan; v 5.3.5, The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, 2014). MannWhitney U test was used, and P value of < .05 represented statistical significance. For the quality assessment, risk of biases

Results

A total of 8 studies 9-11,13,20-22,25 were included in the final quantitative meta-analysis ( Figure 1 ; available at www. jpeds.com), and the details were described in Table I and Tables II-IV (available at www.jpeds.com).

These 8 studies included 2259 subjects and assigned to HFNC (n = 1100), standard oxygen (n = 980), and nCPAP (n = 179). Three studies 13,22,25 compared HFNC with nCPAP, 4 studies 9,11,20,21 compared HFNC with standard oxygen, and one 3-arm study 10 compared HFNC with both nCPAP and standard oxygen. Five studies 9,11,13,21,25 were conducted in patients with acute bronchiolitis, and the other 3 trials 10,20,22 were studied in patients with World Health Organization-defined severe pneumonia. All studies used a flow of at least 2 L/kg/min for HFNC except for the first completed RCT 11 where a conservative flow of 1 L/kg/min was the maximum therapy and another RCT 21 used 1 L/kg/ min as the initial flow rate. Most studies comparing HFNC and standard oxygen were performed in children with respiratory distress and mild hypoxemia (SpO2 >90% on room air), 9,11,20,21 and studies comparing HFNC and nCPAP were conducted in children with moderate-to-severe respiratory distress and severe hypoxemia (SpO2 <90% on room air or requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >90%). 10,13,22,25
Criteria on Treatment Failure

Treatment failure was determined by clinical signs including respiratory rate, heart rate, pulse oximetry, and a need to escalate treatment. The criteria for treatment failure varied slightly among studies and are summarized in Table V (available at www.jpeds.com).
Quality and Heterogeneity

For the 8 included studies, we did not identify any biases in random sequence generation, allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, or selective reporting. Because of the visible and audible differences between the methods of oxygen delivery, none of the studies could be blinded for participants, clinicians, or researchers. This produces challenges for the objective assessment of clinical outcomes, such as treatment failure. However, 7 of 8 studies 911,13,20,21,25 used objective measures and procedures to reduce the risk of ascertainment bias ( Figure 2 ; available at www.jpeds.com). Intention to treat and per-protocol analyses were also reported in all studies. No significant publication biases were detected in the included studies that reported all registered outcomes ( Figure 3 ; available at www.jpeds.com).

No statistical heterogeneities were shown in the primary outcomes ( Figures 4-6 ), but we found statistical heterogeneity in 1 secondary outcome reporting the comparison of HFNC and nCPAP on duration of total respiratory support ( c 2 = 3.01, P = .08, I 2 = 67%) ( Figure 7 ; available at www.jpeds.com).
Outcomes

Probability of Treatment Failure. In children with respiratory distress and mild hypoxemia from bronchiolitis or pneumonia, compared with standard oxygen, HFNC significantly reduced the probability of treatment failure (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.40-0.60, P < .001) (5 studies 9-11,20,21 involving 1978 patients) ( Figure 4 ). After stratification for age, the benefit of HFNC over standard oxygen was consistent (infants age 1-6 months: RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.40-0.69, P < .001, 3 studies 9-11 involving 906 infants; infants age 6-12 months: RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.33-0.67, P < .001, 3 studies 9-11 involving 832 infants; children age 1-5 years: RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.160.83, P = .02, 3 studies 10,11,20 involving 142 children). One study 21 used oxygen mask rather than nasal cannula as standard oxygen, and removing this study from pooled analysis did not change the result (data not shown). A subanalysis of HFNC at a flow rate of 1 L/kg/min and 2 L/ kg/min was compared with standard oxygen therapy, and the probability of treatment failure in HFNC remained lower in both flow groups than standard oxygen ( Figure 8 ; available at www.jpeds.com).

Conversely, the risk of treatment failure was higher with HFNC compared with nCPAP in children with moderateto-severe respiratory distress from bronchiolitis, severe pneumonia, sepsis, asthma, and upper airway obstruction (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.20-2.52, P = .004, 4 studies 10,13,22,25 involving 360 patients) ( Figure 4 ). On stratification for age, nCPAP was superior over HFNC on treatment failure in infants (age 1-6 months) (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.17-2.67, P = .007, 2 studies 10,13 involving 203 infants), but there was inadequate evidence to be conclusive in infants age 6-12 months (RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.30-7.17, P = .64; 1 study 10 involving 45 infants) and children age 1-5 years (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.077.63, P = .80; 1 study 10 involving 52 children).

Probability of Intubation. Overall, rates of intubation were low. No significant differences were found in the probability of intubation between HFNC and standard oxygen (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.56-1.68, P = .91, 4 studies 9-11,20 involving 1872 patients). However, a trend of increased probability of intubation was identified in patients using HFNC, compared with CPAP (RR 1.92, 95% CI 0.96-3.81, P = .06, 4 studies 10,13,22,25 involving 360 patients) ( Figure 5 ).

In the subgroup analysis of infants and children age 1-5 years ( Figure 9 ; available at www.jpeds.com), no significant differences were found between HFNC and standard oxygen (infants age 1-6 months: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.24-2.30, P = .61, 2 studies 10,11 involving 152 infants; infants age 6-12 months: RR 1.64, 95% CI 0.46-5.88,

Similarly, there was no difference between HFNC and nCPAP (infants age 1-6 months: RR 2.41, 95% CI 0.77-7.49, P = .13, 2 studies 10,13 involving 203 infants; infants age 6-12 months: RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.307.17, P = .13, 1 study 10 involving 45 infants; children age 1-5 years: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.07-7.63, P = .80, 1 study 10 involving 52 children).

Mortality. Deaths were reported in only 2 studies, which did not show a significant difference in mortality between HFNC and standard oxygen (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.38-1.91, P = .69, 1 study 10 involving 146 patients). There was a trend of higher probability of mortality in patients with HFNC compared with nCPAP (RR 2.87, 95% CI 0.97-8.54, P = .06, 2 studies 10,22 involving 187 patients) ( Figure 5 ). In the subgroup analysis, no significant differences were found between HFNC and standard oxygen or nCPAP in different age groups ( Figure 10 ; available at www.jpeds.com).

Adverse Events. Compared with nCPAP, HFNC resulted in significantly fewer nasal trauma (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.77, P = .009), but similar apnea episodes (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.50-12.46, P = .26) and no air leak or pneumothorax were observed between the 2 types of respiratory support ( Figure 6 ).
No differences were noticed between HFNC and standard oxygen in apnea episodes (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.20-4.90, P = .99) and pneumothorax (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.06-15.83, P = 1.00) ( Figure 6 ).

Discussion

We found that compared with standard oxygen therapy, HFNC reduced treatment failure in children age less than 5 years who presented with respiratory distress and mild hypoxemia from bronchiolitis and pneumonia, with no difference in the incidence of reported adverse events. However, when compared with nCPAP, HFNC was associated with more treatment failure in infants age 1-6 months with moderate-to-severe respiratory distress from bronchiolitis, pneumonia, sepsis, asthma, and upper airway obstruction. There were fewer other adverse events with HFNC than nCPAP, particularly nasal trauma. These findings were more robust for infants. For children age 1 year or older, studies with larger sample size are needed.

Compared with low-flow oxygen therapy and oxygen mask, HFNC has been shown to improve oxygenation and carbon dioxide elimination 26,27 because of the washout of end-expiratory oxygen-depleted gas 28,29 and the tracheal gas insufflation with fresh gas in neonatal and pediatric patients with respiratory distress. 30,31 This may explain the greater benefit of HFNC over standard oxygen therapy in some patients. Positive airway pressure is also reported as another benefit of HFNC, however, the PEEP generated by HFNC is not as consistent and reliable as that generated by nCPAP. Studies found that PEEP started to be generated 32 and FiO2 began to be stabilized 33 when HFNC flow was set higher than the patient inspiratory flow. However, patient inspiratory flow may change breath by breath, as well as in different disease status, thus the relationship between patient inspiratory flow and HFNC flow is variable. Similarly, PEEP was reported to decrease by approximately 50% when the patient's mouth was open. 32,34 These variations may explain our findings that the clinical response to nCPAP was more favorable than the response to HFNC in moderate-tosevere respiratory distress. 35 However, the small number of participants in the comparisons of HFNC and nCPAP

made this finding weak and inconclusive, although it also accords with the findings in neonatal studies. 17,18

Mil  esi et al identified clinicians' familiarity with HFNC devices as another important factor in the success of HFNC utilization. 36 Access to nCPAP in low and middle income countries is usually limited; however, some simplified bubble-CPAP systems have been developed to resolve this critical problem. 10,37

Wedid not find any significant differences in endotracheal intubation rates between HFNC and nCPAP or standard oxygen, which may be the result of the in-time escalation of respiratory support before endotracheal intubation. In most studies, if treatment failure or deterioration occurred, an alternative method of respiratory support was initiated as a rescue therapy, which may have avoided some intubation and mechanical ventilation. Further studies most were under-powered to detect a difference in the probability of intubation. Similarly, the dilution effect of treatment crossover and the smaller subgroup analysis for those who experienced treatment failure may partly explain the absence of any clear differences in HFNC, nCPAP, and standard oxygen on mortality. Such crossover was a necessary safety and ethical consideration for many of these early trials. 9-11,13,23,25 Therefore, the pooled results of intubation rate is complex and inconclusive, due to the confounding effects of other types of rescue non-invasive respiratory support, and small subgroup sample sizes.

Nasal trauma and discomfort were the main complications reported for patients receiving nCPAP, regardless of the devices used. The incidence of nasal trauma from nCPAP varies from 16% to 42%. 38,39 Longer duration of nCPAP beyond 5 days was a risk factor for developing nasal trauma. 39 However, these findings are reported in neonates and may not be applicable to our study population, among whom the incidence of nasal trauma is unknown. In our meta-analysis, HFNC significantly reduced nasal trauma when compared with nCPAP, which is consistent with the findings reported by Collins et al in neonates, whereby the mean nasal trauma score was significantly lower for infants assigned to HFNC than nCPAP. 40 Nasal trauma was not reported as an adverse event in the included studies comparing HFNC and standard oxygen. No significant differences in serious adverse events, such as apnea or pneumothorax, were detected between the HFNC and nCPAP or standard oxygen groups.

Inoursubgroupanalysis,wefoundthatagewasnotaninfluential factor in treatment failure when comparing HFNC with standard oxygen, however, when comparing HFNC with nCPAP, the superiority of nCPAP over HFNC seems to exist only in infants age 1-6 months, not in infants age 6-12 months and children age 1-5 years. This difference might be due to the fundamental differences of HFNC vs standard oxygen and nCPAP. The major benefit of HFNC over standard oxygen is the dead-space washout effect, which is not significantly affected by age. In contrast, consistency of PEEP is the advantage of nCPAP, although the influential factors of PEEP during HFNC, such as mouth breathing and flow setting are more inclined to be impacted by younger pediatrics. However, only 45
infants age 6-12 months, and 52 children aged 1-5 years were included in one study. 10 This potential difference requires future studies with larger sample size to confirm.

There are several limitations in our meta-analysis. The number of available studies is small, especially in the selected subgroup of children age 1-5 years. We encourage further trials to validate our findings in different contexts. The variation of HFNC gas flow rates, nCPAP pressures, as well as the definition of treatment failure produced heterogeneity. However, the threshold of treatment failure involved escalation to a different mode of oxygen delivery was similar. The heterogeneity of the various healthcare settings, which included emergency departments, general wards, intensive care units, in developed and developing nations where the studies were performed, increases the complexity of the results, including the comparison of HFNC and standard oxygen therapy. The setting may influence the intensity of care provided, the familiarity with HFNC, and the recognition of treatment failure. The inclusion of preterm infants in 3 studies 9,11,13 might complicate the interpretation of the results, but we assume it is not significant as they account for only a small proportion (18%). We did not do an analysis of cost-effectiveness or feasibility in different settings due to the lack of inclusion in most studies, however this is important in many clinical settings.

In the studies we included, 67%-87% of children with respiratory distress and hypoxemia improved with standard oxygen therapy alone. Considering the higher cost and greater complexity of HFNC than standard oxygen therapy, HFNC might not be needed as routine primary treatment for children with respiratory distress and mild hypoxemia. Further studies are needed to identify children likely to deteriorate on standard oxygen therapy, and therefore who would benefit from the early introduction of HFNC. We encourage more studies with pragmatic patient selection, standardized methods, and detailed clinical outcomes to further address and define the role of HFNC in the treatment of infants and children with respiratory failure.

Overall, 67%-87% of children with respiratory distress and hypoxemia improved with standard oxygen therapy alone, so efforts to ensure the widespread availability of oxygen therapy in all locations where children present with respiratory conditions are vital. n
